In the
absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I wish to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs the following question:

What progress has been made in the recent negotiations for the sale of salt codfish to Spain and Portugal?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: STATEMENT ON AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman was kind enough to give notice of this question yesterday. I am now in a position to give a fuller reply than I would have been at that time. A Canadian delegation headed by the deputy minister of trade and commerce has been in Spain for some time carrying on trade negotiations with Spanish officials. My colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) recently went to Spain to conclude the final phases of these negotiations with the Spanish government, and to sign the resulting agreement on behalf of the Canadian government.
I am pleased to inform the house, Mr. Speaker, that an agreement has now been reached with the Spanish government. This agreement is the first direct trade agreement between Canada and Spain. It will be signed today in Madrid by my colleague, Mr. Winters, and His Excellency Martin Artajo, Spanish Minister of Foreign Affairs, and will come into force provisionally on July 1 of this year.
The new agreement provides for the exchange of most-favoured-nation treatment with respect to customs duties and related matters. Both countries undertake not to impose discriminatory import or exchange restrictions, except for balance of payments reasons. Such restrictions must not discriminate between dollar countries. As part of the agreement, the Spanish government has undertaken to make available import licences and dollar exchange for minimum annual imports from dollar countries cf 2,000 metric tons of dry salted codfish. This arrangement will improve and stabilize sales of Canadian salted cod in our traditional Spanish market.
Canada has accorded the following tariff concessions to Spain: the binding of free entry on olives from Spain as from July 1. Formerly, olives were subject to a duty of 17-5 per cent ad valorem. We have agreed to reduce the duty on edible olive oil from 7 [DOT] 5 per cent to 5 per cent and to eliminate the one cent per pound duty on almonds. We are also making a small reduction in the duty on paprika. As mentioned earlier, these tariff concessions become effective July 1, 1954.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to take up about five minutes and no more of the time of the house on this bill. I believe that only by a vastly expanded program of industrial research can we hope to retain those domestic and export markets which are slipping through our fingers every day.
The fact that unemployment today is nearly double what it was a year ago is no mere chance. It is due to the fact that Canadian products are being steadily undersold by products being produced in other countries and which are being generally accepted by the Canadian buying public.
The astonishing part of all this is that what we have experienced so far is as nothing compared with what we will experience when Japan and Germany really get into their stride.
Now, what are we going to do about this? We have got to get costs down so that our products can be competitive with those they are competing with from other countries. How are we going to do it? There is one way, and this is by a greatly expanded research program aimed at two things. One is to develop new and better products with which to compete with these other countries and, secondly, to develop new, better and more efficient methods of producing the products we already produce.
The way to get a program like this started is to set up a committee of parliament on which would be included representatives of labour, management and educational institutions. Such a committee could study and discuss the best means of getting a program such as this under way, and obtaining the best results from it.
Such committees are not new. They have been proved to be a tremendous success in Great Britain and the United States, and there is no reason at all why such a committee would not be just as successful here in Canada. I am sorry, as I am sure most Canadians are, to see that the government has not already set up such a committee following the suggestion made by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) last fall. Much valuable time has already been lost.
One of the reasons Canadian products are being steadily undersold by products from Great Britain and the United States is simply the fact that tremendous and continuous programs of industrial research are carried on in those countries. I believe that industry in this country has been unnecessarily handicapped by the unwillingness of the government to take any action so far in this regard.

Because the government has refused to take action and take this first step toward helping industry to get its costs down, this government must take the responsibility for the fact that Canadian products are continuing to be undersold; that we are losing markets day by day; and that unemployment, compared with a year ago, is steadily increasing in this country.
A glint of hope was given last night by the parliamentary assistant when he intimated that the government might be willing to accept the idea of setting up a committee of this kind. I hope that that is the view of the government, that the government has changed its mind, and that the government has at long last decided to accept the excellent suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Lambton West last fall, and that by the beginning of next session we will see a committee on research set up and under way.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 463, an act to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to supplement or round out the pension benefits provided under the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Defence Services Pension Act by adding to them a scheme of contributory death benefits.
It covers all public service employees who are contributing or who have completed their contributions under the superannuation act and all members of the regular armed forces.
The amount of the death benefit, in the case of public service employees, will be the employee's annual salary adjusted upward where necessary to make it an even multiple of $250, but with a top limit of $5,000. In the case of the armed forces the amounts will be an even $3,000 for persons below the rank of chief petty officer in the navy and equivalent ranks in the army and air force, and $5,000 for all others.
The rate of contribution by all those covered will be 10 cents a month for each $250 of benefit, that is, the rate will be 40 cents per $1,000 per month.
The government, of course, takes full responsibility for this measure, but I should like to say that the general outlines of these proposals were referred confidentially to the national joint council of the public service of Canada. The national joint council made a number of suggestions, most of which have been incorporated in the bill. I would not wish to imply that every member of the national joint council agrees with every detail of the bill, but I can inform the house that the national joint council has endorsed the broad outlines of the plan as a whole. I should also like to record my appreciation of the constructive assistance given by the national joint council in formulating this plan.
Yesterday on the resolution stage the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) asked whether the armed forces had been consulted in connection with this plan. The plan was formulated for the public service in the first instance and representatives of the armed forces then asked to be given a chance
5104	HOUSE OF
Public Service Superannuation Act to participate in the plan. Thereafter all the commands in Canada and abroad were asked for an expression of opinion of a good cross-section of all units under each command as to whether members of the armed forces should participate in a compulsory plan of this nature. Most were in favour of so doing. As regards the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to which the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich also directed his attention, I might say that they are not covered because they already have a group insurance plan of their own in force.
Participation in this added benefit will be obligatory upon all those covered by the superannuation act and upon all members of the regular armed forces. This compulsory feature of the plan is one which is bound to give rise to some individual objections. It has been included by the government only after very careful consideration and with the benefit of the advice of the national joint council.
The plan itself arose in part out of the review which was being conducted as to possible amendments to the Civil Service Insurance Act and in part out of the request of the national joint council and other bodies, for a group plan to provide benefits such as the one being introduced. The remarkably low rate of contribution is made possible only by the fact that this is a compulsory scheme and that those in good health as well as those in poor health are included. In addition to substantially higher rates of contribution, a voluntary scheme would have involved much greater administrative costs. As time went on, larger numbers of those who had not wanted to be under the plan in the first place would wish to participate as their family responsibilities increased or health deteriorated. If these persons were to be included there would have had to be the complicated addition of varying rates of contribution and medical examinations in all fairness to regular participants.
This plan is primarily designed to provide funds which will be readily available to pay the inevitable expenses arising out of or consequential upon the last illness and death of a contributor. The contributions are designed to cover the benefits under the plan on a month-to-month basis. I would not expect any large surpluses to be built up, and there is provision for an actuarial review within five years at which time, if the results warrant it, the rates would be adjusted upward or downward to keep the scheme in financial balance.
While to the younger civil servant or member of the forces who has no dependents now, and who has no present intention of remaining permanently in the public service, the


compulsory feature may seem to be unattractive, it will be possible to remain a participant under the plan by electing to do so upon retirement or withdrawal from the public service provided he has had a minimum of five years of service substantially without interruption immediately prior to that time. In that event, of course, it will be necessary for the individual to keep up the regular payment of contributions which will be higher than those paid while in the service because no government contribution will be payable in respect of those who have retired before they were eligible to receive an immediate annuity under the Public Service Superannuation Act or the Defence Services Pension Act.
The government contribution will take the form of the payment of one-sixth of the benefits of those who die while in the service or who had qualified for an immediate annuity upon retirement. This will replace the present gratuity of two months' salary on death which the government has been paying under section 56 of the Civil Service Act. In the case of those civil servants who are not covered by this scheme, the two months' gratuity on death will still be available under the same conditions as before. A similar basis of contribution will apply in the case of the armed forces, replacing the present interim allowance payable for two months following death of a married member of the forces. Interest will be payable on any balance to the credit of the accounts which are to be set up for those in the public service and those in the armed forces. Assuming normal mortality experience, there should be no net increase in government expenditures as a result of the introduction of this scheme.
One further general point: It will be clear from a reading of this bill that it is not intended to provide for the normal life insurance requirements of individuals. It provides only a reasonable and moderate death benefit of a kind commonly made available to employees by a growing number of large private employers. Public servants, like all other citizens, will continue to make their own provision for their own individual life insurance requirements in accordance with their individual needs and circumstances.
Turning now to some of the details of the plan, I might mention that the amount of the benefit will be subject to reduction of one-tenth of the nominal maximum for that participant for each year that the participant's age exceeds 60. This is subject, however, to an over-all minimum of one-sixth of the salary while the person is still employed. A person who elects to contribute after retirement will be subject to the same reduction

so that there will be no benefit available once that person is 70. In the case of members of the armed forces their earlier retirement age will mean that no reduction would normally apply until after retirement.
In conclusion, I should recall the statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made in the House of Commons on April 30, when he announced that this legislation was to be introduced. He indicated that the government proposed to discontinue the issuance of new individual contracts under the Civil Service Insurance Act. Later that day I issued a statement to the effect that no new contracts of insurance under the Civil Service Insurance Act would be issued unless the medical examination was begun prior to May 1, 1954. This bill contains a section to implement this policy. This step has been taken on the grounds that it is not usual for an employer to provide individual policies for his employees and that the introduction of this new plan of supplementary death benefits provides the best means of meeting the minimum financial needs on the death of an employee over and above the indirect protection given by other legislation. All policies issued under the Civil Service Insurance Act will, of course, remain in full force and effect.
As my parliamentary assistant indicated at the resolution stage, since this bill has a number of technical aspects I believe it can best be considered in detail in the banking and commerce committee; and unless there is serious objections to such procedure I would move that it be referred to that committee at the conclusion of the debate on second reading. Officers of my department and, no doubt, officers of the civil service associations will be available to discuss the bill there.

The first thing that strikes one about it is the title, namely "An act to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act". Actually it has nothing to do with superannuation or pension. Indeed it seems to me that it could 83276-323
Public Service Superannuation Act much more properly have been called an act to amend or indeed to replace the Civil Service Insurance Act of 1893, which was subsequently amended in 1914 and in 1920. I do not wish to make a great point about the title except to say I feel that there is something not quite natural about bringing in these measures and just tacking them on as a schedule to the Public Service Superannuation Act.
Actually it is not clear what the principle of this bill is. Is it the principle to force civil servants to come in and insure themselves? I understand that under the provisions of the present Civil Service Insurance Act only some 13,000 are insured. If you consider that figure and consider the situation if this bill becomes law-it will automatically affect, I suppose, some hundreds of thousands of people -the question of compulsion looms rather large.

While I have noted what the minister said about consultations had with representatives of the service, both military and civil, nevertheless there are those who have been looking after their own insurance, who have been ordering their own affairs and who do not welcome this interference in their lives.
These and other questions, it seems to me, might well be gone into by the banking and commerce committee; and I welcome the fact that the bill is to be referred to that committee. Public Service Superannuation Act
I have given this measure a great deal of my personal consideration. It has been under study for many months, and I am satisfied both that it is a good measure and that the proper place to have it is in the superannuation act. I do not mean that my opinion should prevail necessarily; nevertheless I am convinced that this is so. I do not think anyone has ever accused me of being a socialist. I am convinced that this is not socialization of the life insurance business.
As I said in my opening statement it is intended to provide death benefits, of a relatively small amount, which will take care of the inevitable liabilities which are accumulated in most cases just prior to death.
The superannuation act itself, as the house knows, contains a substantial insurance element. Every superannuation plan which makes provision for a widow or children to receive an annuity after death of an employee or a civil servant, contains an insurance element, in the true sense of the term.
Like my hon. friend from Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson), I like to think I know something about life insurance. In earlier days I used to earn a fair part of my living by advising life insurance companies how to operate, according to the legal aspects of their business. So that I believe I do know something about life insurance contracts.

I am a great believer in insurance. I have a keen regard for any plan that gives security to families by way of pensions and superannuation to civil servants or pensions and insurance plans to industrial workers as well. I have had some experience in that field, and I have always encouraged pension plans so that when people are out of a job or reach maturity they might benefit from some such plan.

The minister says he has given this a lot of study. I have great regard for the minister's judgment on some occasions; in fact, I have a high regard for his sincerity on all occasions, but I do not just agree with him that because he has given it a lot of study it is necessarily a hundred per cent right. He says it certainly is not socialistic and that the principle of it cannot be termed an insurance principle-the amount is too small. Well, amounts rise and fall but principles never change. To my mind, the size of the insurance amount does not alter the principle. He has said that every pension plan has some insurance element in it. That is true. That is the intention, but I submit, Mr. Speaker, there is a unique difference in this. This is not the same as the ordinary superannuation or pension scheme. It is not merely, as the minister says, only a supplement to that. This is a case of where, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) has quite properly said, many thousands are involved in addition to those who are on superannuation or pension schemes today.
The minister says that he has carefully avoided calling it insurance because he does not think it is. I can understand why he would carefully avoid calling it insurance or getting into the insurance business, but I submit that because he carefully avoids calling it that it does not follow that we of the opposition cannot so describe it. We call it as we see it. In so far as pensions and superannuation are concerned, I do feel that the insurance feature of it is one thing, but I do not believe we should have an act passed under which everybody in the civil service and in the armed forces must take their insurance in this way.
I can agree with the Minister of Finance that our insurance companies in this country are doing a grand job. They are among our soundest and best institutions in the country. They have given a fine service to this country by encouraging people to prepare for their old age, sickness, hospitalization and so forth. They have co-operated with industry in an excellent way, and have encouraged industry to look after their labouring men. They have given a fine service in the development of this country and in having money available. Despite what my hon. friends to the left may say, I must agree with the hon. member for Simcoe North that after all service without profit is a misnomer. It is certainly through companies like insurance companies that industry has been able to obtain capital to the extent of $10,000, $12,000 and sometimes $15,000 per man employed in

They are sound; in fact, they are a pattern to many other places where insurance companies have not been as well handled perhaps. I must say that through the government and government regulations our insurance and banking business have been well handled in this country over the many years of that development.
But I do believe that this bill should not now be read a second time but that the subject matter thereof should be referred to the committee on banking and commerce. I say that not merely because the hon. member for Greenwood has moved it; I say that not merely because this party does stand for free enterprise and the encouragement of initiative and genius in our financial setup which I believe has stood the test of time here and has been demonstrated as successful on this whole North American continent, and in fact we might say in the free parts of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in support of the amendment to the effect that the subject matter of this bill be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce. I believe that the debate this afternoon, instead of clearing the air regarding the principle of this bill has to a certain extent clouded the issues. However, I am not going to enter into any discussion as to the advantages of government entering the field of insurance, though I certainly believe that before the committee evidence could be adduced as to which might be the cheapest method of dealing with the matter.
Last night I expressed some doubts as to the wisdom of proceeding with the resolution upon which this bill is based, and since then my doubts have been reinforced by representation made to me from outside the house regarding the desirability of making this form of additional benefits to the superannuation act compulsory. There are many groups in the civil service and in the armed forces who do not appreciate being compelled to take out this new form of benefit.
I think I may point out that the more senior members, either of the armed services or the civil service, have over a number of years been able to build up the security they considered necessary to look after their families after their death. They have been investing their savings in various forms of insurance to augment their pension over a great many years. Many of them are carrying all the insurance their salaries will permit them to carry at the present time. If they are to be compelled to take on another $5,000 that will mean a reduction in their present salary to the extent of the contributions which are necessary, and it will also mean a consequent lowering, though not too great, in their standard of living.
Again, those who have already provided for their families know that their estate will be subject to succession duties when they die. This means that another $5,000 will be added to the estate to be subject to taxation for succession duties when they die, so that instead of the widow receiving $5,000 she may receive only $4,500, the other $500 being deducted in succession duties for a senior member of the services.

There are many forms of group insurance, but I do not believe that any of these group schemes now in existence demand that all employees contribute to that group insurance scheme, so I do not see why it is necessary to insist that every member of the civil service or the armed forces, whether they have already provided for their families after death or not, must contribute to this scheme.
There is also the problem of the junior member, particularly the female members in the civil service and in the armed forces. They regard the provision of an estate after their death as being the responsibility of the male member of their families, and those who do not marry and do not intend to marry at the present time do not see why they should have to put their savings into a form of life insurance rather than into an annuity.
Many young people contribute to life insurance in order that they may have some capital on which they can borrow money. I do not know whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will explain whether an individual will be able to borrow money on the amount of his contribution paid into this particular fund.
Another field of activity was brought out in the debate last night. The parliamentary assistant said that crown corporations could, if they wished, enter into this scheme. That is a field in which various insurance companies have been carrying group insurance policies for these employees in crown corporations, and that will certainly be an invasion into the legitimate field of these insurance companies.
A good deal of emphasis has been laid upon the fact that this is a death benefit designed to assist in the payment of bills connected with the final illness of the contributor. I would like to point out that in many provinces hospital insurance is already provided by governments. For example, in the province of British Columbia there is hospital insurance. Contributions are made in various ways and there are similar schemes in other provinces so that commitments for the final illness may not be particularly heavy, and they are already being provided for through one medium of taxation or another.
Again there are voluntary schemes such as the Blue Cross scheme which provide for the expenses paid during illness. It seems to me that there is every reason to refer the subject matter of this bill to the committee on banking and commerce. The experts can then come before that committee and can explain the necessity for the measure and the committee can hear the objections which are held by various members of the civil service and by members of the armed forces to having to contribute to this scheme.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words at this point. I hesitate to offer any more congratulations to the chairman of the banking and commerce committee in the fear that it would not be good for him. But I must say this that as a new member in the House of Commons and, of course, of the banking and commerce committee, I did appreciate very much the endless courtesy extended by the chairman
[The Chairman.]
and also by the witnesses to a very inexperienced member on the committee trying to play his part in an unaccustomed field.
I found it intensely interesting and extremely educative to be on the committee. I believe I speak for all members when I say that I am sure we benefited immensely from the evidence given by the various distinguished witnesses who appeared before us, and who answered so frankly and so fully the rather groping questions of those who, like myself, were new to that particular field,
I should like for a moment or two to speak about some of the changes made, and the implications of those changes. As the minister has said, the amendment permits the chartered banks to lend money on chattel mortgages. It remains to be seen of course just to what extent the chartered banks will take advantage of that new provision. I, myself, was somewhat in doubt as to whether we were wise in not getting a clearer definition of the legality of the existing method of imposing effective rates of interest on personal loans. Apparently there have been two conflicting legal opinions in that regard, and it is possible that we might have been wiser had we put in operation a course of action that would have resulted in a final court decision in that regard.
There were also in the banking and commerce committee a number of other interesting developments. A point I found most interesting was the very clear evidence that now we have an entirely different banking system from that which existed twenty years ago. I doubt whether anyone in the banking business today would deny that fact for a moment. It was for that reason that some of us in this group who served on the committee pursued the question of the much debated inner reserves. I speak for myself when I say that this was done, not so much from the point of view that here were some hidden profits that malefactors in the banking business were hiding from us but because we felt that the whole concept of inner reserves was an example of, shall we say, a hold-over of thinking from a previous banking system, and that today the arguments which might have been made in favour of inner reserves are no longer valid.
As those who attended the meetings of the committee will recall, the Minister of Finance was extremely careful not to commit the government to any blanket proposition that nowadays the government of Canada cannot afford to let any chartered bank fail. But I think I was not alone in that committee in gathering the very clear impression that it would be extremely unlikely for a government in Canada to let a bank fail

today. In fact that was one of the things that seemed to me to come out most clearly from the hearings of the banking and commerce committee. I was impressed by the fact that today we have an integrated banking system of which the Bank of Canada, the publicly-owned institution, is the one part, and the chartered banks are the other part.
No longer can we ignore the fact that the two functions of the chartered banks-and there are two quite distinct functions-indicate that in Canada we have a somewhat anomalous position with regard to our banking system. Those two functions, of course, are first the guarding of the savings of the general public and making loans to industry, and secondly the distribution, expansion or contraction of the money supply, in co-operation with the Bank of Canada and the government of Canada. Because of this latter function, 1 think the contention that those of us in this group have been making all along, the contention that the banking system inevitably must sooner or later become classified as a public utility is a valid contention.
I would conclude by suggesting that long before the Bank Act comes again before a banking and commerce committee of the House of Commons it will be accepted generally that such a development is in the interests of the orderly development of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I shall detain the house only for a few moments. I approve of the amendments which are being brought before the committee today. However, there was, in my opinion, at least one shortcoming in the Bank Act before it was referred to the committee. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that one of the major weaknesses of our banking system has been its failure to provide long term credit facilities for agriculture. I am afraid that even with these amendments, the act is still not going to provide such facilities.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there are today in Canada a great many farmers who, for one reason or another, cannot go to their bank and get the kind of credit they need. I think this situation is serious, because since the war the price of land has skyrocketed, the price of machinery has gone up, and it is becoming ever more costly to establish a herd of livestock.
Out in western Canada today the price of a half section of land together with equipment has risen to almost $20,000, and though in eastern Canada it is not quite so expensive, young farmers still find the price is so high that they usually find it impossible to purchase a farm.
There is no place under our present banking system where they can obtain long term credit. I am well aware that over the years the government has brought in the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Both of these acts have proved beneficial, but the experience, at least in western Canada, has been that their provisions are too restrictive. Either the down payment required is too high, the terms are too severe, or the ceilings are too low.
I therefore think the time has come, while we are dealing with the Bank Act, to consider whether or not there is something we can do to give Canadian farmers long term credit facilities. We can, of course, extend the provisions of the Canadian Farm Loan Act, or the Farm Improvement Loans Act and I think such a policy might be a good idea. However, may I suggest another alternative.
Earlier this session, parliament amended the Bank Act in such a way that the government now guarantees the losses banks may incur in making a 20 or 30-year loan to urban dwellers on the construction of new homes.

If it is possible to do this for urban dwellers to help them build homes, I do not see why it should not be possible to adopt a similar principle where farmers are concerned. I see no reason why the government could not guarantee bank loans made to farmers over a 20 or 30-year period in the same way for the purchase of farms or equipment.
I think such a policy would give farmers the kind of long term credit they need without being in any way costly to the taxpayers. I hope the minister will give this suggestion some consideration while this act is before parliament.

There was a fundamental change made in the act in 1944 by which it was provided that the Minister of Finance takes the responsibility of determining whether the reserves are excessive. I believe that in the course of the committee's hearings it was established that under present circumstances these reserves could not exceed

The Bank Act
$320 million, which was tantamount to drawing aside the curtain and giving us a peek at the facts. Since that time I have been wondering whether it is necessary any longer to keep all the facts hidden. I wonder whether the minister has not also changed his views a bit on that matter. I believe that was one reason why the inspector general of banks tabled in the committee a report which showed that the aggregate amount under present circumstances could not exceed $320 million. speechtext: I do not think I have. For the first time the inspector general of banks indicated to the standing committee the formula which is used in determining whether the reserves of a particular bank have reached the permitted maximum. He also gave the maximum which would be permitted for all banks under that formula. I think I indicated to the committee that in a case of this kind I would prefer to have too much in those reserves than too little. It might well be that at some later date it might be considered appropriate to break down that information a bit more, but I do think this is a matter with respect to which we should proceed rather slowly. My understanding is that in other commercial countries such as Great Britain and the United States, whose banking systems are most closely comparable to ours, they do not disclose under any circumstances the amount of the banks' inner reserves. I think myself that section 88 has performed a very useful purpose in the history
The Bank Act
of Canadian banking. I feel it has provided credit which might not otherwise have been available. I am also one of those who believe that in due course it may cease to be necessary as a form of security to be taken by banks. I would not be at all surprised if in the next revision or some subsequent revision of the Bank Act it would be found that this was no longer necessary as the country has developed. It is a rather expensive way of taking security. There is a great deal of paper work involved. The banks, themselves, are not particularly keen about it. Nevertheless, as I say, I think it has fulfilled a very useful function over the years. I do not think the time has yet come when we could safely do away with it.

speechtext:
I have one matter I should like to discuss, though I do not know whether I should mention it here or on clause 75. Since 91 is the clause which fixes the ceiling on interest rates, I think I shall discuss the matter now.
Clause 75 is a new amendment which permits banks to lend money on chattel mortgages. I think this idea is certainly a good one, because many Canadians who are today forced to go to small loan companies will now be able to go to the banks and borrow at considerably lower rates. I noticed in the proceedings of the committee that Mr. McKinnon of the Bank of Commerce suggested that the banks could do a more effective job in making these small loans if they were permitted to charge interest rates of one per cent per month. I was not in the committee and there may have been reasons why the suggestion was not desirable. However the argument Mr. McKinnon put forward was simply that the bank's administration costs in connection with these small loans were so high that they needed a higher interest rate to make the proposition economically feasible.

The Bank Act
It seems to me there may be some sense in Mr. McKinnon's argument. If we want to get the banks into the small loan business, if we want the banks to provide a better service to small borrowers, we must let them charge rates which are economically sensible. As I understand the law today, a bank can charge up to 10-46 per cent by discounting the note originally at 6 per cent, and then obtaining monthly repayments. Mr. McKinnon asked for one per cent per month, which would be about 1-5 per cent higher than the present rate. I believe, Mr. Chairman, the house should give careful consideration before passing this 6 per cent ceiling on the chattel mortgage business.
I have had a good deal of experience with this kind of paper financing. Frankly, from what I have seen of it, I doubt if the present rate is going to be sufficiently interesting for the banks to go after the small loan business. I am only speaking personally. I could be wrong, because as I say I was not in the committee when the evidence came up. However I urge parliament to remember that banks, in dealing with this kind of loan, are dealing with risks which are greater than they have in the ordinary loan. Moreover the cost of servicing personal loans is greater, because the repayments come once a month. I certainly think the 6 per cent ceiling should be maintained on standard loans, but I should like the minister to make a statement as to whether or not we might not have more Canadians benefit if the banks were able to make these personal loans now at a slightly higher rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I gave that very careful consideration, Mr. Chairman, but on balance I came to the conclusion I was not prepared to recommend an increase in the maximum permitted interest rate at this time. One reason is that it is quite difficult to distinguish between the different types of loans. While admittedly these so-called small loans to purchasers of individual consumer goods do carry a higher rate of interest, I would be afraid there might be some temptation to get a little higher rate of interest on loans on which perhaps that higher rate was not justified. On balance, therefore, I came to the conclusion we should not at this time raise this permitted 6 per cent maximum.
One other reason, too, was that the banks are now engaged in loans on residential housing, and with the demands on them for ordinary commercial accommodation, I think the result will be that all the resources of the banks will be fairly well utilized in the immediate future. I was, personally, unwilling to recommend an increase in this permitted 6 per cent ceiling. I think the matter

should be studied. Some banks may want to engage in this personal loan business extensively, and others less extensively. I know there is experience in the United States which shows that the rates there, even allowing for escrow deposits and so on, are substantially in excess of the 6 per cent. 1 would not be prepared to take the responsibility of recommending an increase from that figure at this time.

speechtext: With regard to this clause, and the others following in this group, I believe it would be of interest if the minister would make a general statement as to the consolidated stability and general strength of our banking system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
There is no change in substance, so far as these clauses are concerned. I believe there were some improvements in wording. On a number of occasions I have expressed my confidence in the Canadian banking system, which has developed as a result of the process of trial and error that has taken place over a good many years. Some of the defects either in law or in banking management have been eliminated, and today I believe we all agree that we have one of the strongest banking systems in the world. I think, too, that the introduction of a central bank has helped to assure that the banks would be in a more liquid position than they might have been under preceding legislation. I think the very effective work done by the inspector general of banks, as it has been done over a number of years, has contributed to that end.
I know the hon. member for Nanaimo would like me to admit that it is now impossible for a bank in Canada to fail. I am not prepared to make that admission. I think that the responsibility for solvency must continue to be the primary responsibility of the managements of banks, and I think they are discharging that responsibility admirably.
